narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the third decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This lower standing signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.50 it is higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, so this feature pulled the prediction toward passing and helped offset some of the concern. However, it was not enough to overcome the other signals.

Your LSAT score of 33 was the third most important factor and again pushed toward failure. It sits below the 37.18 average of accepted applicants, reinforcing the model’s concern about your readiness for the bar.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of your third-year class rank and LSAT score created too high a risk of first-time failure, even though your strong GPA was a positive note.

What you should do next is straightforward: retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score, then reapply. A stronger LSAT would directly address the two features that most hurt your chances and could flip the prediction in your favor.
